strengths: The paper proposes a simple and well-motivated hybrid model (NIMO) that preserves global linear coefficient interpretation via marginal effects at the mean while adding per-instance nonlinear corrections.
The optimization method based on parameter elimination is technically sound and allows closed-form updates for linear coefficients, with adaptive ridge regularization for sparsity.
The ablation study on feature masking and positional encoding provides useful insight into the model design.
The paper is generally clear, well-structured, and positions the work appropriately against related methods such as LassoNet, NAM, and IMN.
The extension to generalized linear models (logistic regression) is a nice addition and broadens the potential applicability.
weaknesses: The synthetic datasets are generated exactly from the NIMO model class, so the large MSE improvements in Table 1 are expected and do not provide convincing evidence of general expressive power or robustness to model misspecification.

The interpretability evaluation is largely qualitative: aside from a toy example, there is no systematic quantitative evaluation of local explanation fidelity or faithfulness to ground-truth marginal effects across the main synthetic settings.

On real datasets, NIMO is not consistently better than baselines: it is comparable on diabetes and Boston housing, and only clearly best on superconductivity, which weakens the claimed favorable accuracy-interpretability trade-off.

The model cannot capture self-interactions of the form x_j f(x_j) or other nonlinearities not representable as x_j times a function excluding x_j, which limits the claimed expressiveness and is only acknowledged in the conclusion rather than stress-tested experimentally.
The paper claims efficient optimization, but no runtime, complexity, or scaling analysis is provided for the parameter-elimination procedure, especially in higher dimensions.

Feature ranking comparisons rely on SHAP as a pseudo-ground truth, but SHAP is itself a post-hoc approximation and does not guarantee correct feature importance, so these comparisons are not a rigorous interpretability evaluation.
Some reproducibility details are incomplete, such as hyperparameter search ranges, exact model sizes for baselines, and whether code will be released, which hinders full assessment and replication.

strengths: The paper is clearly motivated and addresses an important tension between predictive performance and interpretability in tabular settings.
The proposed NIMO architecture is intuitive: it preserves linear coefficients as marginal effects at the mean while augmenting them with neural-network-based per-instance corrections.

The parameter-elimination strategy and adaptive-ridge formulation provide a technically reasonable way to optimize the coupled linear and neural-network parameters, with a closed-form solution for the linear coefficients.
The sparsity mechanisms, including adaptive ridge/Lasso equivalence and first-layer group regularization, are well explained and potentially useful for feature selection.
The toy example is illustrative and shows that NIMO can recover known coefficients and nonlinear corrections in a controlled setting.
The paper includes comparisons against several relevant baselines, including Lasso, LassoNet, NAMs, and IMNs, and reports competitive performance on some real datasets.
The ablation study on feature masking and positional encoding provides some insight into the design choices, and the overall exposition is generally clear.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: combining a linear model with neural-network corrections, using profile-likelihood-style parameter elimination, adaptive ridge regression, and group sparsity are all existing ideas. The main novelty is a specific masking/positional-encoding design, which is incremental.

The model has a serious expressivity limitation: because g_j excludes the j-th feature, NIMO cannot represent nonlinear main effects of the form x_j f(x_j). Many real-world tabular relationships involve such self-nonlinearities, so the claim of retaining neural-network expressivity is overstated.

Interpretability claims are stronger than the evidence. Only MEM_j = beta_j is inherently interpretable; the per-instance nonlinear corrections h_j are not directly intelligible feature effects. Local marginal effects contain cross-derivative terms involving other features, so the network corrections do not provide transparent local explanations as claimed.

The evaluation of interpretability is weak. Synthetic datasets are generated exactly under the NIMO functional form, which favors the proposed model and does not test whether it recovers general nonlinear structure. Real datasets have no ground-truth effects, and the paper mainly compares rankings or MEM magnitudes rather than quantitatively validating explanation fidelity.

The synthetic experiments use only 200 training samples, and results in Table 1 are reported without variance or confidence intervals. This makes it difficult to assess statistical significance and robustness.

Real-data evaluation is limited: only three regression datasets are used, two of which are small, and no real classification datasets are evaluated despite the logistic-regression extension. Broader tabular benchmarks are missing.

The optimization procedure is not theoretically analyzed in the nonlinear setting. Adaptive ridge is equivalent to Lasso only in the linear model at the optimum; extending it to the coupled nonconvex NIMO objective requires stronger justification and convergence guarantees, which are absent.

Several design choices, such as noise injection into the first layer, are heuristic and justified only by informal statements like 'works very well in practice,' without systematic ablation or theoretical grounding.

The paper does not provide code or a reproducibility statement beyond mentioning PyTorch Lightning; important hyperparameter grids, random seeds, and implementation details are only partially specified.

Ethical concerns around the Boston housing dataset and its controversial 'B' feature are noted but not substantively addressed, even though the model's conclusions about that feature could have sensitive implications.

The comparison to post-hoc explanation methods is underdeveloped. The paper argues that post-hoc methods lack fidelity, but does not evaluate NIMO against established explanation metrics or human studies, so the practical interpretability benefit remains unproven.

strengths: The proposed NIMO model has a clear and elegant formulation: it preserves the interpretability of global linear coefficients via marginal effects at the mean (MEM) while allowing per-instance nonlinear corrections through neural network outputs.

The optimization approach based on parameter elimination is technically sound and practical. It derives closed-form expressions for the linear coefficients in ridge/adaptive-ridge settings and extends the idea to generalized linear models via IRLS.

The use of adaptive ridge regression and group l2 regularization provides a principled way to encourage sparsity in both the linear coefficients and the first network layer, improving interpretability.

The paper includes a reasonable set of experiments: synthetic data for coefficient/nonlinearity recovery, real UCI datasets for predictive performance, comparisons to several interpretable baselines, and an ablation study on feature masking and positional encoding.
The results on synthetic settings are strong, and the real-data results suggest competitive predictive performance with greater sparsity on some datasets.
weaknesses: The model class is significantly narrower than the paper's "expressive power of neural networks" framing suggests. Because g_j excludes x_j and the nonlinearity is only a multiplicative correction to x_j beta_j, NIMO cannot represent univariate nonlinearities such as sin(x_j) or x_j^2 without feature engineering. It primarily captures interactions in a restricted multiplicative form.

The synthetic experiments are generated using the same functional form that NIMO assumes (x_j beta_j(1+g(x_-j))), so they may favor NIMO by construction and do not test out-of-class nonlinear functions. This weakens the central empirical claim of expressive power.

Interpretability evaluation on real data is limited: there is no ground truth for coefficients or explanations, MEM rankings are only compared heuristically to SHAP and other methods, and per-instance explanations are not quantitatively evaluated on real datasets.

Novelty is moderate rather than high. The architecture is closely related to varying-coefficient models in statistics, and the optimization uses known ideas such as profile likelihood/parameter elimination and adaptive ridge regression. The paper does not provide theoretical guarantees or a deep methodological advance.

Experimental coverage is incomplete for a top-tier conference. Most main experiments are regression; classification is relegated to the appendix, real datasets are limited and relatively old, and some results lack exact numeric values or error bars in the main text.

Reproducibility is not fully demonstrated. No code or artifact is referenced, baseline hyperparameter tuning is not detailed, and the shared-network implementation with positional encoding and the g(0)=0 constraint is somewhat under-specified.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, such as accurately recovering local explanations generally. The paper itself acknowledges that features with self-interactions may not be captured, which directly limits the proposed method's generality.

strengths: Introduces a simple and intuitive hybrid model that preserves the global interpretation of linear coefficients at the mean while allowing nonlinear per-instance corrections via neural networks.

Develops a parameter-elimination optimization strategy with closed-form updates for the linear coefficients and an adaptive-ridge extension to logistic regression, enabling sparsity and efficient gradient-based training.
Synthetic experiments effectively illustrate recovery of ground-truth coefficients, sparsity patterns, and nonlinear correction functions, with strong predictive performance in low-data regimes.
Real-data results on diabetes, Boston housing, and superconductivity are competitive with strong baselines, and local explanations align reasonably well with SHAP in the appendix.
Includes useful ablations on feature masking, positional encoding, and group penalty, and honestly documents a key limitation regarding self-interactions.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the model is closely related to varying-coefficient models, contextual Lasso-style methods, and existing interpretable hybrids such as LassoNet and IMN; the optimization uses known profile-likelihood/adaptive-ridge ideas adapted to NIMO.

The interpretability claims are somewhat overstated: excluding x_j from g_j does not make x_j contribute only through beta_j, since other correction networks g_i (i != j) can still depend on x_j. MEM_j = beta_j holds only at the feature mean, so beta_j is not a global feature effect except at that point, and the proposed local coefficients ignore cross-derivative terms.

Scalability is not adequately addressed: because g_j depends on x_{-j}, computing all d corrections still effectively requires d forward passes per instance; for high-dimensional data this may be costly, and no runtime, memory, or complexity comparison is provided.

Evaluation is limited: synthetic data-generating processes are exactly within NIMO's model class, so performance advantages are expected; real-data experiments cover only three main datasets (plus regression-only PMLB results in the appendix) with no real classification benchmark and no quantitative interpretability metrics such as coefficient-recovery error or sparsity F1.

The optimization and training recipe contain heuristic components: group l2 penalty plus noise injection on the first layer is not theoretically justified, the training loss in Algorithm 1 appears to have a typo (lambda||gamma|| instead of lambda||gamma||^2), and hyperparameter sensitivity is not deeply analyzed.

Reproducibility and ethics are incompletely addressed: no code release is mentioned, and although Boston housing's controversial feature is noted, broader ethical and societal implications are not discussed in depth.

strengths: Introduces a simple and intelligible hybrid architecture that keeps global linear coefficients while allowing per-instance nonlinear corrections through a shared neural network with positional encoding.

The optimization strategy based on parameter elimination is technically plausible: it profiles out β using closed-form ridge/adaptive-ridge updates and can be extended to logistic regression via IRLS.
The synthetic experiments show that, when the data-generating process matches NIMO’s functional form, the model can recover ground-truth coefficients, nonlinear corrections, and sparsity patterns.
The paper includes some useful ablations (feature masking, position encoding, group penalty) and an honest limitations section on self-interactions and basis expansion.
The model can achieve competitive predictive performance on several real datasets and has a clear intended use case in interpretable tabular regression/classification.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. The architecture resembles varying-coefficient models and earlier neural-linear hybrids; the closed-form β elimination is essentially profile likelihood, and the adaptive-ridge/Lasso equivalence is a known result. The paper does not position itself against a sufficiently broad related-work landscape.

The central interpretability claim is overstated. MEM_j = β_j only at the standardized mean; this is not a global population-level feature effect for nonlinear models. The paper calls MEMs global interpretations while later acknowledging that MEM can be misleading, and the proposed local contributions c_j(x) ignore cross-derivative/interaction terms, so they are not faithful decompositions in general.

Synthetic evaluation is biased in favor of NIMO. The generated functions are of the exact form x_j β_j (1 + g_j(x_-j)), so recovering them is expected and does not demonstrate robustness to model misspecification, arbitrary interactions, or realistic tabular nonlinearities.

Real-data evaluation is weak. Only a few small/outdated datasets are used, Boston housing is controversial and includes a sensitive feature (“B”) without any fairness/ethical analysis, and the main paper lacks statistical significance testing or large-scale benchmark results. PMLB results are relegated to the appendix and are not integrated into the claims.

Baselines are not convincingly tuned or compared. Some methods use default hyperparameters or implementations, while NIMO’s hyperparameters are selected by grid search. The comparison does not isolate whether gains come from the architecture or from optimization/regularization choices.

Optimization claims are unsupported. There is no convergence analysis, complexity analysis, sensitivity study, or discussion of differentiating through the closed-form inverse. The algorithm’s efficiency is asserted rather than demonstrated, and Algorithm 1 contains at least one apparent typo (λ||γ|| vs. λ||γ||²).

The sparsity mechanism in the first neural-network layer is heuristic and not tied theoretically to the global interpretability claims. Noise injection and group penalties may work empirically, but no principle guarantees that sparse first-layer weights correspond to meaningful interactions or to β sparsity.

Reproducibility and presentation need work. Hyperparameter grids, baseline training protocols, code availability, and compute costs are not fully specified. References are sloppy/duplicated, and several citations are malformed, making the paper feel insufficiently prepared for a top-tier venue.

Claims about post-hoc explanation fidelity are not directly validated. The paper criticizes post-hoc methods for lacking fidelity, yet its own local explanations are validated mainly through SHAP scatter plots rather than quantitative fidelity metrics, user studies, or ground-truth local effects on real data.

strengths: Introduces a simple and intuitive nonlinear extension of linear regression where each coefficient is modulated by an input-dependent neural correction, preserving the linear coefficients as marginal effects at the mean after standardization.
Develops a nontrivial optimization scheme via parameter elimination and adaptive ridge regression, with closed-form updates for the linear coefficients and an extension to GLMs via IRLS.
Provides controlled synthetic experiments showing recovery of true coefficients, nonlinear corrections, and first-layer sparsity, with ablations validating feature masking and positional encoding.
Real-data experiments show competitive predictive performance, especially on the superconductivity dataset, and the paper discusses limitations and ethical/feature concerns for Boston housing.
weaknesses: The global interpretability claim is overstated: MEM is evaluated at the mean, not averaged over the data distribution, and β can be misleading for pure interactions without linear main effects, which the model cannot represent without introducing spurious main effects; the limitation section only considers self-interactions.

Synthetic experiments are generated from the NIMO functional form, so strong MSE advantages partly reflect inductive bias; synthetic results lack multiple seeds/error bars, and classification experiments are limited.

Real-data evaluation is narrow: only a few small/medium tabular regression datasets, no real classification, and missing comparisons to several strong interpretable baselines such as EBM, NODE-GAM, and IME; real-data interpretability is assessed mainly via SHAP consistency rather than ground-truth or user study.

Optimization is not theoretically grounded: no convergence guarantees are provided, Algorithm 1 appears to contain a minor loss typo (λ||γ|| vs λ||γ||²), constraint handling relies on a Lagrange penalty rather than projection, and the per-iteration computational cost of the closed-form solve is not analyzed.

The nonlinear correction networks remain black-box MLPs, so local explanations are limited to modulation factors/contributions and are not necessarily human-intelligible; no code or reproducibility link is provided.
